what_its_for: Rituximab-arrx is used to treat certain types of cancer (such as non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and certain autoimmune conditions (such as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis). It works by targeting and destroying specific white blood cells called B-cells that may be causing harm in your body.
how_to_take: This medication is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly injected into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or healthcare professional will give you this treatment in a clinic or hospital setting. You should never try to give this medication to yourself at home. Each infusion can take several hours, so plan to spend significant time at the clinic on treatment days. You will be monitored closely during and after each infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose and schedule for you based on your specific condition, body size, and overall health. Doses are typically given once a week for several weeks, or once every few weeks, depending on what you are being treated for. Always follow your doctor's dosing schedule exactly. Do not skip or change appointments without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: Since this medication is given in a clinical setting, missing an infusion appointment is something to take seriously. If you need to reschedule or miss an appointment, contact your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one. Your doctor will advise you on the best way to get back on track with your treatment schedule.
storage: You will not need to store this medication at home, as it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals. At the clinic or pharmacy, it is stored in a refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should be protected from light and must not be frozen. Once it is mixed and prepared for infusion, it should be used within 24 hours if kept in the refrigerator, or within 12 hours at room temperature.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as the chickenpox, MMR, or nasal flu vaccine) during and after treatment, as your immune system will be weakened. Talk to your doctor about which vaccines are safe. Try to avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections. Avoid crowded places when possible to reduce your risk of getting sick. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as this medication can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 12 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: fever, chills, or signs of infection; chest pain or tightness; difficulty breathing or shortness of breath; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; severe skin rash, blisters, or sores; unusual bleeding or bruising; sudden confusion, vision changes, or difficulty walking or talking (these could be signs of a rare but serious brain infection); severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting; or yellowing of the skin or eyes. Also tell your doctor if you notice any new or worsening symptoms between treatments.
when_it_works: How quickly this medication works depends on what condition is being treated. For some cancers, you may not notice changes right away, and it may take several weeks to months before you see the full benefit. For autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, some patients notice improvement within a few weeks, but it may take several months for the full effect. Your doctor will monitor your progress through regular check-ups and lab tests to see how well the medication is working for you.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): This medication can be used in older adults, but they may be at a higher risk for serious side effects, including infections. Close monitoring is important. Pregnancy: This medication can harm an unborn baby and should not be used during pregnancy unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 12 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medication passes into breast milk. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Children: The safety and effectiveness in children have not been established for all conditions. Talk to your child's doctor for guidance. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how your body handles the medication.
